A freight invoice can be mathematically correct and still be linked to the wrong shipment or service.

Before recalculating anything, match the invoice to the shipment identifier, carrier, account, freight mode and service level. Then locate the governing commercial terms and check for replacements or prior credits.

The first deliverable is a traceable record—not an estimated refund.

What is the FIRST thing to check on a freight invoice?

Not the total. The shipment identity.

Match the bill to its shipment or PRO number, carrier, account, service level and the records showing what actually moved. Only then compare the charge with the governing terms.

posts.text:
Two invoices contain the same shipment number. That is a reason to investigate—not yet proof of duplicate payment.

Trace the original bill, any correction or replacement, the credit memo and the payment ledger. Ask whether the second document replaces the first or represents a separately authorized charge.

A useful finding identifies the final economic obligation and what, if anything, remains paid twice.

See the duplicate-freight-charge evidence guide:

posts.text:
TWO INVOICES ≠ TWO OVERPAYMENTS.

A corrected bill can leave a misleading duplicate in an export. Before flagging it, connect four records: original invoice → replacement bill → payment → posted credit.

Only a reconciled remaining duplicate is a candidate for a supported finding. A carrier correction already received isn't a fresh recovery.

Save this four-document check.

A liftgate accessorial appears on an LTL bill. Which evidence would show whether it belongs?

Start with the agreement: is the service included, separately billable or conditional? Then inspect the delivery notation, proof of delivery and any correction or prior credit.

A charge label tells you what was billed. It doesn't establish whether the service occurred or the separate fee was authorized.

Review the four-slide accessorial evidence guide:

posts.text:
LIFTGATE FEE: WHAT WOULD YOU ASK FIRST?

Swipe through the evidence chain:

1 / What did the signed rate terms permit?
2 / Was liftgate actually required or provided?
3 / Does the delivery record support the event?
4 / Did the carrier already correct or credit it?

A bill line alone cannot answer those questions. Sometimes the fee is appropriate.

posts.text:
A fuel surcharge can use the correct formula and still reference the wrong effective schedule.

To independently reconstruct it, identify the signed rate authority, fuel index and lookback period, eligible transportation base, effective percentage table and rounding method.

Don't substitute a newer online index—or simply choose the lower percentage—without the governing agreement.

Use RETALLY's carrier-rate review checklist:
https://www.retallyrecovery.com/carrier-rate-audit?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=retally_feb2027_controls&utm_content=fb_fuel_index_window

ONE LOAD. TWO FUEL SURCHARGE TABLES.

The lower table isn't automatically the valid one.

Confirm the contract, shipment date, applicable fuel index period, eligible base charge and rounding. Amendments and incorporated tariffs can change the answer.

If the controlling source is missing, the result is an unresolved question—not recovered money.

Save this rate-authority checklist.

What does a $0-upfront freight audit actually establish?

An agreed eligible population can be reviewed without an initial audit fee. That does not guarantee that a discrepancy exists, that a carrier will accept a claim or that any refund will follow.

Separate recovery work requires written authorization. Fees are governed by eligible value actually recovered under the agreed terms—not hypothetical savings.

Would a second reviewer be able to understand a freight-billing dispute without asking for missing records?

A useful case file contains five elements: shipment and invoice identity; the challenged charge; controlling rate authority; service evidence; and a reproducible expected-charge calculation, reconciled against prior credits.

A supported calculation makes a claim reviewable. It isn't carrier approval or recovered funds. Customer authorization precedes any recovery outreach.

See the dispute-package sequence:
https://www.retallyrecovery.com/freight-overcharge-dispute-process?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=retally_feb2027_controls&utm_content=fb_dispute_packet

That package supports review. It doesn't guarantee a carrier will approve a claim.

Freight invoices and rate contracts can contain private pricing and account details. Social comments and DMs are not the appropriate route to share them.

An initial conversation can stay non-sensitive: carrier categories, freight modes, general billing periods and scope. Confidential documents require an agreed secure transfer method and appropriate authorization.

RETALLY's public worksheet uses illustrative or anonymized figures and doesn't upload the amounts.

WHAT SHOULD YOU SEND IN A FREIGHT-AUDIT DM?

General questions about scope are fine. Private invoices, rate agreements, account numbers and payment details are not.

Agree on the review and a secure transfer route before exchanging sensitive files. The public worksheet runs locally with sample or anonymized amounts only.

Share this reminder with your freight AP team.

posts.text:
A carrier marks a freight dispute "approved." Finance still has a separate question: what value was actually received and retained?

Record the approved amount, posted credit memo, usable offset or refund, and any later reversal as distinct events tied back to the shipment and supported finding.

A report that counts approvals as cash—or ignores a reversed credit—overstates the financial outcome.

Read RETALLY's evidence and settlement standard:
https://www.retallyrecovery.com/freight-recovery-evidence-standard?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=retally_feb2027_controls&utm_content=fb_net_credit_status

"CREDIT APPROVED" IS A STATUS. NOT CASH.

Keep a separate record for:

• Supported billing finding
• Carrier approval
• Usable posted credit or refund
• Any adjustment or reversal

Only eligible net value actually realized belongs in recovery totals under the written terms. A reversal should change the total.
